checks: The old almost-everywhere integer midpoint forces equal parity of both endpoint bases, hence equal restricted masses in every class. Because the finitely many original base levels are separated, E_{i,r} is the support of the restricted measure, and any base appearing there has positive restricted mass. A zero-mass class has empty supports, zero ceiling and the zero coupling.

For q≥1 the harmonic-power expression is continuous and coordinatewise nondecreasing on the positive quadrant and its zero extension is continuous because it is at most 2^q min(t,s). The q=0 minimum has the same regularity. The product of the compact support parts maps continuously to the compact attainable midpoint set. Upper semicontinuity of the composed ceilings gives attained maxima on nonempty fibers and the subsequence argument gives upper semicontinuity of the output envelope on the ambient space.

In a positive class with q>0 the common direction gives the global orthogonal coordinate map (z,x)↦((z,proj_{L⊥}x),proj_L x) in orthonormal coordinates. Endpoint supports are compact, their auxiliary base sets are finite real sets, and intrinsic μ agrees there with counting times Euclidean q-area. The physical p is integer for every product pair, so all product midpoints lie in S by convexity. Auxiliary coordinates themselves need no integrality.

For each output p the same auxiliary offset works for every pair giving p, and its affine q-plane equals aff C_p. Consequently σ_P restricted to K=(E_{-,r}+E_{+,r})/2 is precisely the restriction of physical μ in the chart. Equal weights, compact K_i=E_{i,r}, f_i=a_i, full sets E_i=K_i and g=c_r on K meet every accepted variable-density hypothesis, including finite integral and the pointwise product inequality. The isometry and its inverse preserve all finite convex tests.

When q=0 each nonempty sampled fiber is a singleton and the support product is finite in the full physical ambient space. The atom ceiling theorem gives H_0 and the needed convex order with no area factor. Different parity classes can reach the same output; summing the dominated physical measures adds their capacities, and within one class the envelope is a maximum even for colliding pairs. Fiberwise constant a_i reduces its bound to the corresponding positive base-pair maximum.

For unit ceilings the envelope is the indicator of the attainable set. A supporting hyperplane through p forces both bases of a pair with midpoint p onto that hyperplane by zero averaged slack. At integer p their parities lie in the image of p+Λ, and Λ∩2ℤⁿ=2Λ because halving an even vector stays in the direction subspace. The number is exactly 2^rankΛ for the whole affine lattice and bounds the number of contributing classes. Noninteger p has no attainable midpoint.

An interior projected base lifts to an interior point by the strict combination of one known ambient interior point and a lift beyond the given base. Thus it has a full d-dimensional fiber. This also covers the projected interior in ℝ⁰, so q<d forces n≥1 and puts each sampled base on the projection boundary. A supporting hyperplane there has direction rank at most n−1.

The full-dimensional example has 2^n input fibers per marginal of unit measure. Coordinatewise, the only even-sum ordered pairs from {0,1}×{1,2} are (0,2) and (1,1), giving the all-ones output base and forcing total mass 2^n onto one fiber of measure one. Pairing identical continuous coordinates gives density 2^n and an admissible old coupling. The argument includes the empty product n=0 and the counting case d=0. The exact complement enumeration was also checked in dimensions 0 through 6.

The degenerate example uses any q-dimensional unit-volume convex body K, or a singleton when q=0. The wedge C is full-dimensional by strict inequalities in the nontrivial coordinates. Since 0<ε<1, every integer t equals zero and then v=0, so the sampled fibers are copies of K with trace dimension q. The same complement forcing in n−1 coordinates and diagonal continuous pairing yield total mass and constant 2^(n−1) on one fiber of measure one, also for n=1 and q=0.
